title: ZOLOFT (sertraline hydrochloride) tablets, for oral use; ZOLOFT (sertraline hydrochloride) oral solution: full prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved labelling, published in DailyMed (National Library of Medicine); structured product label version 7, published 24 July 2025, effective 8 August 2023; boxed warning and sections 5, 6, 8, 10, 12.2 and 14
funder: not stated. The document is prescribing information approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and published by the labeller, Viatris Specialty LLC.
result: Boxed warning: antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours in paediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. In pooled placebo-controlled trials of antidepressants in about 77,000 adults and over 4,400 paediatric patients, drug-placebo differences in patients with suicidal thoughts or behaviours per 1000 treated were 14 more under 18 years, 5 more at 18 to 24, 1 fewer at 25 to 64 and 6 fewer at 65 or older; no suicides occurred in paediatric studies; whether the risk extends beyond four months is unknown. Warnings: serotonin syndrome, potentially life-threatening, also when SSRIs are used alone; increased risk of bleeding events from ecchymosis to life-threatening haemorrhage, to which aspirin, NSAIDs, antiplatelet drugs and anticoagulants may add, and a less than 2-fold increase in postpartum haemorrhage with exposure in the month before delivery; mania or hypomania in 0.4% of sertraline-treated patients in trials that generally excluded bipolar disorder; discontinuation reactions including dizziness, electric shock sensations, anxiety, confusion, hypomania and seizures; seizures (patients with seizure history excluded from trials); angle-closure attack from pupillary dilation in people with untreated narrow angles; hyponatraemia, with serum sodium below 110 mmol/L reported and severe cases with seizure, coma, respiratory arrest and death, often through SIADH, with elderly, diuretic-treated and volume-depleted patients possibly at greater risk; QTc prolongation and torsade de pointes reported after marketing, and in a thorough QTc study in 54 healthy adults at twice the maximum dose (about 3-fold steady-state exposure) the largest mean placebo-corrected QTc increase was 10 ms (upper 90% bound 12 ms); sexual dysfunction (ejaculatory delay or failure, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, delayed or absent orgasm), which may not be spontaneously reported. In pooled 8- to 12-week trials (3066 sertraline, 2293 placebo): insomnia 20% against 13%, somnolence 11% against 6%, decreased appetite 7% against 2%, tremor 9% against 2%, hyperhidrosis 7% against 3%; in men (1316 against 973) ejaculation failure 8% against 1%, decreased libido 7% against 2%, erectile dysfunction 4% against 1%; in women (1750 against 1320) decreased libido 4% against 2%; the label states that these estimates may underestimate the actual incidence of sexual adverse experiences. Paediatric MDD trials (n=373, 10 weeks): about 1 kg weight difference, weight loss above 7% in about 7% of sertraline-treated children against 0% on placebo. Galactorrhoea is listed among premarketing adverse reactions with an incidence below 2%. Postmarketing reports include hyperprolactinaemia, gynaecomastia, SIADH, severe liver events including fatal liver failure, pancreatitis, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, pulmonary hypertension and rhabdomyolysis. Third-trimester exposure: neonatal complications requiring prolonged hospitalisation, respiratory support and tube feeding, and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (background 1 to 2 per 1000 live births). Overdose: seizures, coma, QRS and QTc prolongation, serotonin syndrome. Efficacy in MDD rests on two short-term trials (6 and 8 weeks) and one randomised withdrawal trial in which 295 responders to 8 weeks of open sertraline continued sertraline or switched to placebo for 44 weeks: relapse 11 (8%) against 31 (39%). In two further PTSD trials sertraline did not differ significantly from placebo; post hoc analyses showed essentially no effect in men.
